slides.title: Recap: Requirements Engineering Foundations
bullets: Requirements capture what the system must do
Good requirements are testable and traceable
Week 4 covered elicitation, analysis, and specification
slides.notes: Briefly remind students of the requirements engineering lifecycle: elicitation, analysis, specification, and validation. Emphasize that clear, unambiguous requirements are the prerequisite for any executable specification. This recap connects Week 4 material to today's focus on turning those requirements into machine‑readable contracts.

slides.title: What Is Spec-Driven Development?
bullets: Specification is the single source of truth
Code is generated or validated against the spec
Reduces documentation drift by making the spec authoritative
slides.notes: Spec‑driven development (SDD) treats the specification as the authoritative artifact. Instead of writing code first and documenting later, the spec defines the contract; implementation is then generated or continuously validated against it. This approach reduces documentation drift because the spec drives both client and server code, and any change must be reflected in the spec before code is updated. The key idea is a closed loop: spec → generate/validate → deploy.

slides.title: Core Principles of Spec-Driven Development
slides.notes: The four pillars of SDD are: (1) design the contract before any implementation, (2) express the contract in a machine‑readable format (OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL, Protobuf), (3) use tooling to generate stubs, clients, or run conformance tests, and (4) store the spec in version control so it can be reviewed like code. These principles ensure that every public method matches the agreed interface.

slides.title: Major Spec-Driven Frameworks
slides.notes: Three dominant frameworks cover the main API styles: OpenAPI for RESTful HTTP services, GraphQL SDL for flexible query‑based APIs, and Protocol Buffers for high‑performance RPC (often with gRPC). Each provides a language‑agnostic schema, tooling for code generation, and validation libraries. The choice depends on team expertise, performance needs, and ecosystem.

slides.title: OpenAPI 3.1 Structure
slides.notes: An OpenAPI document starts with metadata (info, servers). The paths object maps HTTP endpoints to operations. Reusable data models live under components/schemas, enabling DRY definitions. Security schemes describe authentication (API keys, OAuth2). Vendor extensions allow tool‑specific metadata without breaking the standard.

slides.title: GraphQL Schema Definition Language
bullets: Type system: scalar, object, interface, union, enum
Root operation types: query, mutation, subscription
Custom directives can carry metadata such as authorization hints or caching policy
slides.notes: GraphQL SDL defines a strong type system. The schema must declare root query, mutation, and optional subscription types. The only built‑in directive is @deprecated; however, developers frequently define custom directives (e.g., @auth, @cacheControl) to attach application‑level metadata. These directives are not part of the GraphQL spec but are widely used by tooling.

slides.title: Protocol Buffers (proto3) Basics
bullets: Scalar types: string, int32, bool, bytes, etc.
slides.notes: Protobuf uses a compact binary wire format. A .proto file declares messages (data structures) with numbered fields and services (RPC interfaces). The protoc compiler reads the .proto file and generates client/server stubs in languages such as Go, Java, Python, and TypeScript. Field numbers must remain stable for backward compatibility.

slides.title: Worked Example: User Login API – OpenAPI

figure.caption: OpenAPI 3.1 snippet for a login endpoint
figure.code:
openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: Auth API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /login:
    post:
      summary: User login
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              required: [username, password]
              properties:
                username:
                  type: string
                  minLength: 3
                password:
                  type: string
                  writeOnly: true
                  minLength: 8
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Successful login
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  token:
                    type: string

slides.notes: Walk through the spec line by line: the info block, the /login path with a POST operation, a requestBody that references a schema requiring username and password. Note the password field uses writeOnly: true and minLength instead of a non‑standard format. The 200 response returns a token. Show how a tool like openapi-generator can produce a server skeleton that enforces this contract.

slides.title: Worked Example: User Login API – GraphQL SDL
bullets: Define Login mutation input and payload
Schema is executable with GraphQL servers

figure.caption: GraphQL SDL for login mutation

slides.notes: Explain the SDL: a Query type with a login field that takes username and password and returns AuthPayload. AuthPayload contains a token and a User object. The custom @auth directive illustrates how teams attach authorization hints (e.g., required roles) without extending the GraphQL spec. Tools like Apollo Server can read these directives for middleware.

slides.title: Worked Example: User Login API – Protobuf
bullets: Use protoc to generate gRPC stubs

figure.caption: Protobuf definition for login service

slides.notes: Show the .proto file: package declaration, service with a single RPC, request/response messages, and a nested User message. Emphasize that field numbers (1,2,…) are part of the wire format and must not be reused. Running protoc with the gRPC plugin produces client and server interfaces in the target language, guaranteeing that the generated code matches the spec exactly.

slides.title: From Requirements to Executable Specs
bullets: Map each use case to an API operation
Choose spec framework per service style
Write spec, review, version, and baseline
slides.notes: The translation process starts with the requirements document. For each use case, define the external interface (REST endpoint, GraphQL mutation, gRPC method). Select the appropriate spec language. Author the spec collaboratively, run linting (e.g., spectral for OpenAPI), and store it in version control. The spec then becomes the baseline for code generation and contract testing.

slides.title: Ensuring Interface Conformance at Runtime
bullets: Protocol Buffers compiler (protoc) for code generation
slides.notes: Runtime conformance is achieved by (1) generating client SDKs from the spec so callers cannot send invalid payloads, (2) validating incoming requests against JSON Schema using libraries such as ajv, (3) using protoc to compile .proto files into type‑safe stubs that reject mismatched messages, and (4) embedding these checks in CI/CD so any drift fails the build. This closes the loop between spec and implementation.

slides.title: Check: Spec-Driven Development Principle

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the core principle of spec‑driven development?
options: Write code first, then generate documentation from the implementation.
Treat the specification as the authoritative contract and generate or validate code against it.
Use informal comments in code as the primary source of API contracts.
Maintain separate documentation and code repositories with manual sync.
quiz.explanation: Option B captures the contract‑first mindset: the spec is the single source of truth and drives code generation or validation. Option A is the traditional code‑first approach, which leads to drift. Option C relies on informal comments, not machine‑readable specs. Option D describes a manual process that spec‑driven development aims to eliminate.

slides.notes: This quick poll checks that students grasp the fundamental shift from code‑first to spec‑first. Discuss why the other options are common misconceptions.

slides.title: Check: Runtime Conformance Tools

quiz.question: Which tool is a JSON Schema validator, and which is the Protocol Buffers compiler?
options: ajv validates JSON Schema; protoc compiles .proto files.
protoc validates JSON Schema; ajv compiles .proto files.
Both ajv and protoc validate JSON Schema.
Both ajv and protoc compile .proto files.
quiz.explanation: ajv is a popular JSON Schema validator for JavaScript/TypeScript. protoc is the Protocol Buffers compiler that generates code from .proto definitions; it does not validate JSON Schema. The other options confuse the roles of the two tools.

slides.notes: Reinforce the distinction between schema validation (ajv) and protobuf compilation (protoc). This mirrors the correction needed for the earlier slide.

slides.title: Summary: Spec-Driven Development Frameworks
bullets: Spec is the authoritative contract; code follows
OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL, and Protobuf cover REST, GraphQL, gRPC
Worked examples showed login API in all three formats
Runtime conformance via generated clients, ajv, protoc, and CI
slides.notes: Recap the four key takeaways: (1) the spec‑first mindset, (2) the three major frameworks and their sweet spots, (3) concrete translation of a login use case into each spec language, and (4) the toolchain that keeps implementation honest. Remind students that Assignment 2 will require them to produce an executable spec for a given requirements document.
